raw_response:
I will not turn everything upside down at the start of the year. On 70 mu, I still need grain for steady cash flow, so I will keep wheat-maize as the backbone and put more money only where vegetables and fruit can bring higher return. Last year’s way is always my base. If a rate worked and the neighbors who manage well used something close, I will stay near that and only push a little higher where I think yield is worth protecting.

For wheat, I will keep 35 mu. In our place, if wheat is short of fertilizer early, I can hardly make it back later, so I will feed it a bit on the safe side. I will use an improved variety, rotary till after the previous crop, put most phosphorus in the base fertilizer, split nitrogen into base plus jointing stage, and give about 4 irrigations if the weather is normal. After wheat, I will follow with maize on the same 35 mu. Maize needs enough fertilizer for ear size, and with well irrigation I can hold the stand if summer rain is uneven. I will use hybrid seed, keep fertilizer a little stronger than last year rather than weaker, and spray 3 times if insects and leaf disease show up.

Cotton, chili, and watermelon bring cash, but they also eat money fast. Cotton on 15 mu is still worth keeping because it spreads risk. I will not starve potassium there, because weak potassium shows in boll setting. Chili on 10 mu needs the tightest management among these crops. I will water more often, feed it steadily, and spray many times because once disease and thrips get ahead, the field turns bad quickly. Watermelon on 10 mu I will handle carefully with enough base manure-equivalent fertilizer and more potassium; if vines look too lush, I will hold back nitrogen later. Cauliflower I will put on 10 mu in autumn after early land opens up. That crop likes fertility and water both to be steady. I will not gamble with low fertilizer on cauliflower because if heads stay small, the price cannot save it.
